paragraphs: Bernheim’s Forest Giants page says that in 2019, for the forest’s 90th anniversary, Danish artist Thomas Dambo built three giant sculptures in the Arboretum from recycled wood gathered in the region. The family story he wrote, “While the Weather Got Better,” places Little Elina and Little Nis with their mother, Mama Loumari. In the poem, Elina looks at the sky and a feather falls, a sign of good luck.

A March 21, 2019 Bernheim account says Little Elina forms rocks into the shape of a giant feather, while Little Nis looks into Holly Pond and Mama Loumari rests against a tree. Dambo used recycled wood from pallets, fallen trees, bourbon barrel staves, and scraps from the Louisville Slugger Museum & Factory. Named wood sources include Allen’s Logging and Sawmill, Best Made Pallets, and Speyside Cooperage in Shepherdsville.

Current visiting notes ask guests to start at the Visitor Center. The giants form a 2-mile round trip, and visitors may climb only on Little Elina’s feet and hands, no higher. Messages go in her writing capsule. The visit page lists seasonal grounds hours of 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and a recommended admission of $15 per car.

name: Wooldridge Monuments
title: Wooldridge Monuments in Mayfield
description: Eighteen stone figures made for Henry G. Wooldridge between 1892 and 1899 fill a plot in Maplewood Cemetery.
subtitle: Eighteen stone figures in Maplewood Cemetery
lede: Eighteen stone sculptures in Maplewood Cemetery commemorate Henry G. Wooldridge, his family, and animals he hunted with. He is the only person buried in the plot.

facts.label: Carvers
facts.value: Tomb by Pryor and Radford; Will Lydon of Paducah Marble Works claimed 12 figures

paragraphs: The National Register nomination describes 18 stone sculptures in Maplewood Cemetery that commemorate the life, interests, and closest relatives of Henry G. Wooldridge. Work ran from 1892, when he bought the lot, to 1899, when he died. Only his remains are in the enclosure. The plot measures about 33 by 17 feet on a hillside visible from the cemetery entrance.

The nomination says a marble obelisk, a limestone vault with a rifle in relief, an Italian marble portrait of Wooldridge on a 6-foot base, and a limestone figure of him on the horse Fop form the center. Fourteen local limestone figures surround them, including brothers John H., W. F., and Alfred N. Wooldridge, a fox, two hounds, and a deer. A contemporary source named the dogs Towhead and Bob. The tomb was ordered from Pryor and Radford Monument Works in Mayfield, and stonemason Will Lydon of Paducah Marble Works later claimed 12 of the figures.

Mayfield-Graves County Tourism calls the group “The Strange Procession That Never Moves,” gives the cemetery address as 611 North 5th Street, and says the gates are open 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily. It dates the figures from 1892 until Wooldridge’s death on May 30, 1899, notes that only he is buried there, and says the monuments and the Confederate Memorial Gate are on the National Register. A Kentucky Historical Society marker at the cemetery lists his mother Keziah Nichols, brothers, sisters, great-nieces Maud and Minnie, the dogs, deer, fox, and the horse Fop, and says the central marble image was carved in Italy.

paragraphs: Gambit Weekly says a commission chaired by Richard Foster was formed in 1951, and New Orleans sculptor Angela Gregory designed the monument. The bronze, 26 feet tall, was cast in Paris. Bienville stands with Father Athanase Douay on his left and a Native American figure on his right. It was dedicated on April 24, 1955, outside the Union Passenger Terminal on Loyola Avenue. Speakers included the French and Canadian ambassadors, Gov. Robert Kennon, Mayor deLesseps Morrison, and Archbishop Francis Rummel.

The Historical Marker Database transcribes the base: Jean Baptiste LeMoyne de Bienville, born Montreal, February 23, 1680, died Paris, March 7, 1767, Founder of New Orleans 1717, with homage of Louisiana, Canada, and France. It says the Louisiana Purchase Sesquicentennial Commission erected the monument in 1955. The marker is at the south end of Bienville Place, north of Conti Street, between Decatur and North Peters. description: A bronze Frémiet Joan of Arc, given by France and erected in 1972, now stands on the 900 block of Decatur Street.
h1: Joan of Arc, Maid of Orleans
subtitle: Frémiet’s bronze at Place de France
lede: A bronze equestrian Joan of Arc, one of the duplicates of Emmanuel Frémiet’s sculpture, stands at Place de France on Decatur Street. It was erected in New Orleans in 1972 and moved to the French Market in 1999.

facts.label: Current site
facts.value: Place de France, 900 block of Decatur Street

facts.label: Moved
facts.value: October 1999, from the foot of Canal Street

paragraphs: The Historic New Orleans Collection says this statue is one of many duplicates of a piece created in 1875 by French sculptor Emmanuel Frémiet at the request of Napoleon III. It arrived in the United States in 1958, when a New York company bought it and offered it to New Orleans. Mayor Chep Morrison could not pay. French President Charles de Gaulle, with the cities of Orléans, Paris, Reims, and Rouen, bought the figure and gave it to New Orleans. It stayed in storage until 1972, when it was erected at the foot of Canal Street. In 1999 it was moved to the French Quarter, flanked by antique cannons that had arrived in 1958. HNOC says it now stands on the 900 block of Decatur Street.

New Orleans Historical says the French Quarter figure is one of nine similar statues cast by Frémiet in the late 1800s. It came to New Orleans in 1958, remained in storage about 14 years while the city faced a $36,500 price, and stayed warehoused after de Gaulle paid in 1964 until it was erected in 1972 at the Rivergate. In October 1999 it moved to Place de France in the French Market. The page gives the place as Place de France, Decatur Street, New Orleans, LA 70116.

paragraphs: NOLA.com’s July 3, 2022, account says the bronze of a young woman seated on a fountain near Decatur Street is titled Michelle and made her debut in 1984. She had been removed after red paint and glued decoration and was bolted back after restoration by Zito’s Plating and Polishing Works for the French Market Corporation. The article says she is dressed in summery shorts and a sheer blouse and is sometimes called the mermaid, though she has no tail.

Gayle de la Houssaye modeled for the statue in the early 1980s. Perret made plaster casts of her body. He named the sculpture after his daughter Michelle, not after the model. A caption says the figure began as a nude and was clothed for public display. Perret said he stained the bronze brown, with a pale blue-green blouse and darker green shorts. The article tells readers to look for Michelle where Madison Street intersects the river wall, not far from Café du Monde.

subtitle: A Garden of the Americas figure on Basin Street
lede: A statue of Benito Juárez, president of Mexico from 1858 to 1872, stands at 1200 Conti Street on the Basin Street neutral ground. Mexico gave the figure in 1965, and it was dedicated in 1972.
paragraphs: The Wikipedia entry for the New Orleans statue says Juan Fernando Olaguíbel sculpted the figure of Benito Juárez, president of Mexico from 1858 to 1872. Juárez lived in New Orleans during two periods of exile. The statue was part of Mayor Chep Morrison’s 1957 plan for a Basin Street median called the Garden of the Americas, which also came to include monuments to Simón Bolívar and Francisco Morazán. Mexico gave the Juárez statue in 1965. It was dedicated on May 17, 1972, the hundredth anniversary of Juárez’s death, by the XII Mexico–United States Interparliamentary Conference. The page gives the location as 1200 Conti St, New Orleans, LA 70112.

Verite News, on October 9, 2024, published a photograph captioned as the Benito Juárez statue on Basin Street and said that until recently three Hispanic-hero statues stood on the Basin Street neutral ground. It says Juárez’s statue was a gift from the Mexican government and that he twice fled Mexico to live in New Orleans. The same article says the Bolívar statue had just been placed in storage. It still presents the Juárez figure as standing on Basin Street.
